title: St Andrew (30 November)
hook: the first called, the one who brought his brother, near the start of Advent
tomorrow: Year three close: the story and the circle

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thanksgiving: Paul giving thanks in the storm, and your line was for all good gifts.

"What seek ye?" In John's Gospel, in the King James words, Jesus turns round and asks it of two men who have been walking behind him. Their teacher, John the Baptist, had just pointed at him and said, "Behold the Lamb of God!" So they followed. They don't have a clever answer. They ask where he's staying. He says, "Come and see." And they spend the rest of that day with him. John's Gospel names one of the two: Andrew. And the next thing Andrew does is go and look for his brother. The church keeps his day on the thirtieth of November, near the start of Advent.

Then, John says, "He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ. And he brought him to Jesus." First findeth. Before anything else, he gets his brother. Jesus is about to give that brother a new name: Cephas, a stone. We know him as Peter. And John calls Andrew simply Simon Peter's brother. In the Orthodox tradition he is the First-Called: in John's telling, he follows Jesus before Peter arrives. Watch what he keeps doing. A huge crowd on a hillside, nothing to eat, the disciples worried. It's Andrew who notices a boy: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" He doesn't solve the problem. He just brings the boy, and the little he has, to Jesus. Later, in Jerusalem, some Greeks come asking to see Jesus. They ask Philip. Philip tells Andrew, and Andrew and Philip go and tell Jesus. A brother, a boy, a group of strangers: each time, Andrew is bringing someone. There John's story of him ends. Tradition says he traveled far to preach and died on a cross shaped like an X, and that cross now sits on the flag of Scotland, where he's the patron saint. His day near the start of Advent fits him: the season of waiting opens with the man who said, we have found him, and went to get someone else.

Think of one good thing you've found, a walk, a choir, a quiet church, a book, a kitchen table where people are kind, and then of one person who might need it: not the easiest to ask, but the one who came to mind first. Picture yourself asking plainly, with the words Andrew first heard: come and see. If you pray, pray for that person by name; if you don't, just hold them in mind.
St Andrew. Simon Peter's brother, the one who kept bringing people to Jesus, remembered on the thirtieth of November.
Your line: we have found him. Andrew's first thought was his brother. Until tomorrow.

notes: Claims rule: the thirtieth of November comes from the index title. 'The First-Called' (Protokletos) is the Orthodox title, explained from John 1:40–41; confirm.
Tradition statements (traveled to preach, X-shaped cross, the saltire on Scotland's flag, patron saint of Scotland) are marked 'tradition says' but are not in the cited text. Confirm or soften.
'Often called simply Simon Peter's brother' reflects John 1:40 and John 6:8.
Matthew 4:18 and Mark 1:16 have Simon and Andrew called together by the sea; the lesson follows John's account and says 'in John's telling'. Confirm.
John 6:9 is spoken by Andrew per John 6:8. The 'huge crowd' and 'the disciples are worried' summarize John 6:5–7 (Philip's reply).
Original: εὑρήκαμεν (John 1:41). The English 'eureka' connection is deliberately left out under the etymology rule.
